subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Teaching Business Communication: Competence, Approaches & Management
Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback

subjective.question: What is Business Communication? Define Business English.
subjective.answer: Business Communication is the communication which takes place at the workplace, in an educational setting, a corporate office, or in a government job. Business English is an umbrella term for a mixture of general everyday English, general Business English, and ESP (English for Specific Purposes). The objectives of general English and Business English are the same, but the context is different: in general English one learns the basics — the mechanics of grammar, composition and vocabulary — while in Business English one builds upon what was learned in general English for workplace purposes.

subjective.question: What are the two components of a Business English course?
subjective.answer: A Business English course has two components: (1) Language knowledge, which reflects the formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and the sound system; and (2) Communication skills, in which we activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels.

subjective.question: Describe the five phases of the development of ESP.
subjective.answer: ESP has undergone five main phases of development: (1) The Concept of Special Language — Register Analysis (1960s and early 1970s): the basic principle was that each field has its own particular register. (2) Rhetorical or Discourse Analysis: attention was given to language above the sentence level, i.e. how sentences are combined in discourse to produce meaning. (3) Target Situation Analysis / Needs Analysis: existing knowledge was applied by analyzing the target situation and identifying its linguistic features. (4) Skills and Strategies: the attempt was to look below the surface, to the thinking processes that underlie language use. (5) Learner-centered Approaches: the learner and his needs are placed at the center of course design.

subjective.question: Why should Business Communication be seen as an approach and not a product?
subjective.answer: Business Communication teaching is not a matter of teaching a 'specialized variety' of language, it is not just a matter of business words for business students, and it is not different in kind from any other form of language teaching. Business Communication is not the teaching of a particular language, nor does it consist of a particular type of methodology or material. It should therefore be taken as an approach to language learning which is based on the learner's needs, rather than as a product.

subjective.question: How can Business English learners be grouped or categorized?
subjective.answer: Learners can be grouped: (1) According to experience — pre-experienced learners (no experience of the business world), job-experienced learners (experience of the business world, with precise ideas about what they need), and general business-experienced learners (who fall between the two). (2) According to their level in the organization's hierarchy. (3) According to national culture, since different cultures have different traditions and values regarding learning and education. (4) According to need — some learners have very specific needs, e.g. joining a multinational project. (5) According to language level — beginners, advanced, level three, etc.

subjective.question: Discuss the roles of a Business English teacher as trainer, coach and consultant.
subjective.answer: Teacher as Trainer: a trainer is someone who is required to change a person's behavior or ability so that he can do a specific job; training is job-oriented, while teaching is person-oriented. Teacher as Coach: coaching involves helping the learner to better understand his or her own strengths and weaknesses and to plan accordingly; it is related to learner autonomy, where the learner takes full responsibility for his or her learning. Teacher as Consultant: a consultant is an expert who is brought in because his or her skills or know-how are not available in the organization; in Business English this expertise can include the ability to analyze communication and communication needs, or to recommend a training supplier.

subjective.topic: Teaching Business Communication: Competence, Approaches & Management
subjective.question: Differentiate between linguistic competence, discourse competence and intercultural competence.
subjective.answer: Linguistic competence deals with elements of language at a basic level; it tends to focus on language out of context, on isolated chunks of language. Discourse competence deals with language in use: discourse describes how people interact with each other within context. Intercultural competence includes the ability to deal with, and be sensitive to, differences in how other cultures do things; from a business point of view, the aim may even be to recognize and utilize those differences in order to create something which adds value for the business or its customers.

subjective.topic: Teaching Business Communication: Competence, Approaches & Management
subjective.question: What is Communicative Language Teaching (CLT)? State its main features.
subjective.answer: Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) aims to develop learners' ability to use language to communicate. Its main features are: language is seen not just as a set of linguistic items to be learned, but as language in use via functions; when considering functions, we focus on how we use a language, as opposed to what we know about a language; meaning takes precedence over form; and fluency can take precedence over accuracy.

subjective.topic: Teaching Business Communication: Competence, Approaches & Management
subjective.question: What is Task-Based Learning?
subjective.answer: In Task-Based Learning, learners are encouraged to activate and use whatever language they already have in the process of completing a task. Task-based learning stimulates a natural desire in learners to improve their language competence by challenging them to complete meaningful tasks. It is a strong form of communicative language teaching that focuses on how learning takes place.

subjective.topic: Teaching Business Communication: Competence, Approaches & Management
subjective.question: State the principles of Scientific Management and the six functional areas of business operations identified by Classical Organization Theory.
subjective.answer: Scientific Management is based on the principles of: management as a science, i.e. finding the best method; scientific selection of workers; and scientific education. Classical Organization Theory (Henri Fayol) divided business operations into six interdependent and related functional areas: (1) Technical, (2) Commercial, (3) Financial, (4) Security, (5) Accounting, and (6) Managerial.

subjective.question: What is needs analysis? What is its aim?
subjective.answer: Needs analysis is the first stage in Business Communication course development. Its aim is to collect and examine critically the information about the current situation (where the students are at present) and the target situation (where they would like to be at the end of the teaching). Understanding the difference — the training gap — between these two situations leads to the course design: syllabus, methods, constraints and learning strategies. There is no single best way to do a needs analysis and no hard and fast rules for it.

subjective.question: Differentiate between necessities, lacks and wants in needs analysis.
subjective.answer: Necessities are the type of need determined by the demands of the target situation — what the learner has to know in order to function effectively in the target situation. Lacks are what the learner does not yet know: to decide them, we need to know what the learner knows already, and the gap between the target proficiency and the existing proficiency is called the learner's 'lack'. Wants are the learners' own views: learners may have a clear idea about the necessities of the target situation, and they will certainly have a view as to what they want from the course.

subjective.question: What is a language audit?
subjective.answer: A language audit is a large-scale needs analysis designed to look at an organization and work out its strengths and weaknesses in terms of communication in English. It directly influences all decisions regarding syllabus, materials, methodology and evaluation.

subjective.question: What is a placement test? Write down its characteristics.
subjective.answer: A placement test is a test designed to provide a comparison with other learners (or with known standards or benchmarks) so that learners can be placed with others having similar needs and ability. Its characteristics are: (1) Validity — it should test what it is designed to test. (2) Face validity — the test or questionnaire should appear to be what it is supposed to be, i.e. what is being assessed. (3) Authenticity — the test should reflect the target language. (4) Reliability — it should be reliable, so that if different testers do the same test, the result should be the same.

subjective.question: What is means analysis?
subjective.answer: Means analysis is a description of the training environment: what is available in terms of equipment, materials, facilities and time — and, perhaps more importantly, what is not. Points to consider include what facilities and equipment are available, how much time is available to design the course, how much time is available for training, and at what time of day learners will be available. Means analysis normally produces lists which have an important bearing on the cost of the course.

subjective.question: What are SMART objectives?
subjective.answer: Objectives should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. They specify what needs to be achieved and answer six questions: Who is involved? What do I want to accomplish? Where (identify a location)? When (establish a time frame)? Which requirements and constraints apply? And Why — the specific reasons, purpose or benefits of accomplishing the goal. To determine whether an objective is measurable, one asks: How much? How many? And how will I know when it is accomplished?

subjective.question: Differentiate between teaching/business objectives and performance (behavioral) objectives.
subjective.answer: Teaching and business objectives do not normally specify what the learner will be able to do at the end of the course; they are designed to give the teacher useful guidelines, and they may use technical words which learners may not be familiar with. Performance (behavioral) objectives, on the other hand, specify what the learner is expected to do, under what conditions, and to what level or standard; such objectives use expressions like 'will learn…' and 'will be able to…'.

subjective.question: What is a syllabus? Why do we need a syllabus?
subjective.answer: A syllabus is a list which specifies all the things that are to be taught in the course for which it was designed — e.g. whether it is designed for beginner-level students, for 2nd-semester students, or for IT students. We need a syllabus because it: has a cosmetic role; is an ordered document, essential and easier in the beginning and less important and difficult later; provides a criterion for material selection; provides a practical division of language, assessment and activities; and provides confidence to teachers and learners by making the language learning task appear manageable. In Business English teaching, the focus of the syllabus should be on using language to perform tasks, not just to talk about it.

subjective.question: Differentiate between raw (authentic) materials and published materials. Also state the advantages and disadvantages of using course books.
subjective.answer: Two types of materials can be used: (1) raw materials or authentic materials, e.g. newspapers and reports; and (2) published materials, e.g. course-books. Authentic materials bring the real world into the class and motivate learners by making the task realistic and useful for their future workplace. Advantages of course books: they save the teacher's work; the teacher doesn't have to choose the lesson and the activities; they provide a solid framework; and many course books include comprehensive teacher's guides and resources. Disadvantages of course books: they can get outdated easily; their cultural content might be inappropriate in certain contexts; and they might be based on different assumptions about language learning.

subjective.question: What is framework material? Write down its advantages.
subjective.answer: Frameworks create a situation where the learner is pushed towards using specific language in order to complete the task assigned. A framework consists of a diagram, a simple outline, or a list of key words which can be used as a prompt. Its advantages are: it is easy to produce; it generates relevant language; the learner can focus on meaning rather than form; it can be used with all levels of learners; it is economical — the cheapest material available; it is convenient to use, easy to carry, pack and stack; it provides guidance for inexperienced teachers; and it supports learner autonomy, as learners can learn, monitor and review with autonomy.

subjective.question: What does the term 'authentic' denote? What are the advantages of authentic materials?
subjective.answer: The term 'authentic' denotes that the texts were written for purposes other than language teaching and learning. The aim of using authentic texts and tasks is to bring the real world into the class. Authentic materials can be real commercial documents, newspaper articles and clippings, and recordings of meetings and conversations used in the workplace; they can be accessed from emails, contracts, reports, presentations, voicemail messages, and audio and video recordings of real interactions. Their advantages are: they bring the real world into the classroom; they lead to motivation and interest; and they help the teacher understand the needs of the learners.

subjective.topic: Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback
subjective.question: Describe the six flexible stages of a Business English lesson.
subjective.answer: A Business English lesson can be seen as having six flexible stages: (1) Input — text and information about a business. (2) Presentation — language points, e.g. grammar, vocabulary, functions and pronunciation. (3) Practice — students get a chance to practice these forms and patterns through controlled exercises. (4) Communication points — related to communication tasks, looking at models for a particular communication mode to raise awareness of procedures, behaviors and associated language. (5) Practice — practice of the above. (6) Output Task — production of the language; stage six presents a flexible lesson plan which can be varied according to the teacher's teaching style, the learners' learning style and the available resources.

subjective.topic: Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback
subjective.question: How are learning styles classified? Also describe the four learning styles of Honey and Mumford.
subjective.answer: Learning styles are classified into four types of learners: (1) Auditory learners, (2) Visual learners, (3) Tactile learners — who learn through manipulation of resources, such as writing, drawing, building a model or conducting a lab experiment, and (4) Kinesthetic learners. The four learning styles by Honey and Mumford are: (1) The Activist — learns by doing the task. (2) The Theorist — learns the language by understanding the underlying theory. (3) The Pragmatist — learns by practicing in a controlled environment. (4) The Reflector — learns by watching others do the task.

subjective.topic: Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback
subjective.question: Differentiate between learning styles and learning strategies. Also name the types of learning strategies.
subjective.answer: A learning style (Oxford) is the general approach preferred by the student when learning a subject, acquiring a language, or dealing with a difficult problem; style is natural. Strategies, by contrast, can be purposively taught — they are the characteristics we want to stimulate in students to enable them to become more proficient language learners, and they are directly connected to the learning styles of the learners. The types of strategies are: (1) Metacognitive strategies — planning (previewing, paying attention to main ideas), monitoring (self-checking one's comprehension) and evaluating (developing the ability to evaluate one's own task). (2) Cognitive strategies — summarizing, induction, imagery, auditory representation and making inferences. (3) Social/Affective strategies — cooperating, clarifying (asking questions) and self-talk (reducing anxiety by talking positively to oneself).

subjective.topic: Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback
subjective.question: What is feedback? Describe its two components.
subjective.answer: Feedback is information given to the learner about his/her performance with the objective of improving performance. To be effective, feedback needs to be constructive, balanced and reasonable. It has two components: (1) Assessment — in which you simply inform the learner how well or badly he/she has performed, and give a grade like 70% or a comment like 'good' or 'fair'. (2) Correction — in which more specific information on the learner's performance is given through explanation; it tells what the learners did right and what was wrong.

subjective.topic: Tutoring a Course: Lesson Planning, Learning Styles & Feedback
subjective.question: Write down the guidelines for giving feedback.
subjective.answer: The guidelines for giving feedback are: practice is more important than feedback; team feedback is better than feedback provided by one person; immediate feedback is more effective than delayed feedback; the focus of feedback should be according to the lesson objective; and it is better to give feedback on a few points which can be retained.

subjective.question: Describe the teaching/training styles identified by Marshall and Wheeler.
subjective.answer: Marshall and Wheeler identify five teaching styles: (1) The Listener — prefers the trainee to talk more than the trainer, and wants the trainee to be self-directed and autonomous. (2) The Director — is well organized, tells students what to do, and is the final judge of everything. (3) The Interpreter — separates himself from the learners and observes, and uses theory as a foundation. (4) The Coach — allows learners to evaluate their own progress and uses trainees as a resource. (5) The Consultant — is an expert who gives advice, analyzes and carries out assessment of courses to see whether objectives are met or not.

subjective.question: Discuss the qualities of effective communication: clarity, conciseness, accuracy and ethics.
subjective.answer: Clarity: the ultimate aim of good communication is clarity; if a letter, email or text message is unclear, problems can occur — one should provide specific, quantified information and use easily understandable words, and note that passive constructions and abbreviations, acronyms and jargon can create problems. Conciseness: conciseness saves time, aids clarity, and makes writing appealing. Accuracy refers to grammatical and contextual correctness; if communication is clear and concise but incorrect, it will mislead the audience and destroy credibility. Ethics: ethical communication entails being honest about products and services; the communicator has an ethical responsibility to convey correct and true information, and the ethical principles for technical communicators include legality, honesty, fairness, confidentiality, quality and professionalism.

subjective.question: What are the barriers to listening? Also write the keys to effective listening.
subjective.answer: Listening is a conscious, selective process, unlike hearing, which is involuntary. The barriers to listening include: physical barriers; psychological barriers; language problems; interrupting the speaker; and noise. The keys to effective listening are: stop what you are doing; do not talk; make eye contact; be objective; and ask questions.

subjective.question: What are the constituents of effective meetings? On what does the success of a meeting depend?
subjective.answer: The constituents of effective meetings are: (1) People — the people involved and their being aware of their role in it; (2) Procedure — the steps and stages and their management; and (3) Results — the outcome of meetings. The success of a meeting depends on: communicating the purpose effectively; satisfying expectations; and clarifying the outcomes.

subjective.question: What is negotiation? Write down the constituents and stages of an effective negotiation.
subjective.answer: Negotiation is a special meeting in which parties need each other's agreement in order to achieve an effective result. Negotiation outcomes or objectives may be competitive and win-lose, with directly opposite goals. The constituents of an effective negotiation are: people, planning, the results, and language. The stages in negotiation include: (1) Preparation, (2) Relationship building, and (3) Information gathering. Common contexts for negotiation are buyer-seller, employer-employee and budget allocation.

subjective.question: Explain the process approach to writing. Also differentiate between coherence and cohesion.
subjective.answer: The process approach to writing is a dynamic process based on three steps: (1) Prewriting — examining the purpose, determining goals, considering the audience, and deciding what action you want from your audience; data can be gathered through mind mapping, brainstorming, outlining and researching. (2) Writing — drafting the document, ensuring the elements of structure. (3) Rewriting — revising the document for adding details, deleting wordiness, simplifying words, enhancing tone and reformatting. Coherence involves creating a logical argument or a sequence which makes sense to the reader. Cohesion is about how sentences connect with each other to form a sense of unity, through grammatical devices such as conjunctions, pronouns and lexical items.
